title: Fact check: the viral reel pitting $23 billion in student debt against the Iran war gets the numbers mixed up
dek: The $23 billion is real but was never blocked. The plan Republicans did stop was about $430 billion, and the Supreme Court killed it on legal grounds, not cost. The war has cost more than $40 billion, and Hormuz is still far from open.
body:
A text-on-screen reel making the rounds on Instagram the night before the midterms sets two numbers side by side. Biden tried to wipe out $23 billion in student debt, it says, and Republicans blocked it in court on the grounds that the country could not afford it. Meanwhile, it continues, the United States has spent $40 billion on the war with Iran and still has not gotten the Strait of Hormuz open. Imagine, it concludes, if that $23 billion were being spent by Americans at home.

The reel's broad point about priorities is a matter of opinion, and people will weigh it differently. Its factual claims can be checked. One of them mixes up two different student debt stories, one understates the war's cost, and one is broadly right with caveats.

## Claim one: the $23 billion that Republicans blocked

There is a real $23 billion student debt figure from the Biden years, but it is not the program Republicans blocked, and it was not blocked.

The number matches the settlement in Sweet v. Cardona, a 2019 class action brought by borrowers who said mostly for-profit colleges had defrauded them. The Biden Education Department agreed to settle in 2022, and a federal judge approved the deal that November. It was first described as roughly $6 billion for about 200,000 borrowers [4][5]. Lawyers for the borrowers now put its eventual value at about $23 billion in discharges and refunds for more than half a million people, largely because roughly 179,000 additional borrowers applied for relief between the deal's signing and its final approval [3][6].

The settlement's challengers were not Republican officials. Three for-profit schools tried to stop it. The Supreme Court declined to halt it in April 2023, and the Ninth Circuit rejected the schools' appeal in November 2024 [4][5]. This year the Trump Education Department, now named in the case as Sweet v. McMahon, sought to delay relief for the later group of applicants, citing limited staff and arguing the payouts would be an unfair burden on taxpayers. A unanimous Ninth Circuit panel rejected that request in July [3][6]. So a Republican administration did push back on part of the $23 billion, partly on cost grounds, and lost. Delivery has been slow: about $12 billion had reached nearly 300,000 borrowers as of an April court filing, and the borrowers' lawyers have asked the court to hold the department in contempt, with a hearing set for this week [22][23].

The program Republicans did block in court was much larger. In 2022, Biden announced a one-time cancellation of up to $20,000 per borrower for about 43 million people, a plan the Supreme Court put at roughly $430 billion [1][2]. Six states led by Nebraska sued, and on June 30, 2023, the court struck the plan down 6-3 in Biden v. Nebraska [1].

The reel's description of why it was struck down is where it goes most clearly wrong. The court did not rule that the country could not afford the plan. Chief Justice John Roberts, writing for the majority, held that the HEROES Act, the 2003 law the administration relied on, lets the education secretary waive or modify loan rules but does not authorize rewriting the program to cancel hundreds of billions of dollars in debt. The court also invoked the major questions doctrine, which requires clear authorization from Congress for actions of vast economic significance [1][2]. Missouri was allowed to sue because the state-created loan servicer MOHELA stood to lose fees [2].

Cost did run through the politics around the plan. Republican lawmakers framed their opposition to Biden's relief efforts as protecting the taxpayer who never took out a loan, and the current Education Department argues it is unfair to make Americans who never went to college or already repaid their loans cover others' debt [7][8]. That is a fair description of the political case against cancellation. It is not what the Supreme Court decided.

Biden's administration did cancel a large amount of debt through other routes, including Public Service Loan Forgiveness, fixes to income-driven repayment and fraud claims like Sweet: more than $183 billion for about 5 million borrowers by January 2025 [20]. His follow-up attempt at broad cancellation under a different law was withdrawn by his own administration in December 2024 [24], and his SAVE repayment plan was blocked by the Eighth Circuit and then ended in a December 2025 agreement between the Trump Education Department and Missouri [7].

## Claim two: $40 billion on the war with Iran

The reel's war figure is low. The United States and Israel began strikes on Iran on February 28, 2026 [18]. In an estimate sent to Congress, the Pentagon put the cost to American taxpayers at $47.1 billion as of October 16: about $29 billion in munitions, about $12 billion in operations and about $6 billion in lost or damaged equipment. That total does not include damage to U.S. bases [9][10].

The reel's $40 billion is in line with estimates from the summer. The Congressional Budget Office estimated about $38 billion through August 1, plus $2 billion to $3 billion for each additional month [11]. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told senators in July that the military's costs would reach roughly $37.5 billion by September, and outside analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and the American Enterprise Institute produced estimates between about $35 billion and $42.5 billion in June [12].

Longer-range estimates run far higher. Harvard's Linda Bilmes has projected costs approaching $1 trillion once veterans' care, interest and reconstruction are counted, and Brown University researchers estimate Americans have paid nearly $80 billion more for gasoline and diesel because of the war [12]. Those figures measure something broader than the Pentagon's bill, and they are not what the reel cites.

The administration and its supporters argue the cost buys security. The White House says the campaign's aims are to destroy Iran's missile forces and navy, cut its support for proxy groups and ensure it never obtains a nuclear weapon, and it describes the results as a decisive success [17]. In an assessment published on the war's first day, CSIS analysts said the strikes might reduce Iran's near-term ability to build a weapon, while noting that a stockpile of highly enriched uranium was unaccounted for [18].

## Claim three: Hormuz still is not open

This is the reel's most accurate claim, with a caveat. The strait is not closed outright, but traffic is a small fraction of normal.

Before the war, about 125 large commercial ships a day passed through [13]. Shipping data firms counted roughly 15 to 17 a day in October [14][15]. Gulf oil flows had recovered to more than 80 percent of prewar levels in September before falling again as attacks surged [13]. The International Maritime Organization recorded 29 attacks on ships in the first three weeks of October, the most in any month since March [15].

U.S. Central Command disputes the idea that the strait is lost. It says American and partner forces control the waterway, that the main shipping lanes are clear of mines and that more than 3,000 ships have transited with U.S. support over six months [25][26]. Iran, for its part, treats a full reopening as a bargaining chip. On Monday it proposed an accelerated plan to reopen the strait in exchange for lifting the U.S. blockade and sanctions, guarantees against new strikes and a regional ceasefire, as talks mediated by Qatar and Pakistan continued. President Trump has said the talks are going fine while leaving open the possibility of further strikes after the election [16][21].

## The comparison itself

The reel's closing line treats the two numbers as interchangeable piles of money. The scale is worth knowing. The federal government spent about $7.4 trillion in fiscal 2026 and ran a deficit of about $2 trillion [19]. Against that, $23 billion is about 0.3 percent of annual spending and the war's official $47 billion is about 0.6 percent. Biden's blocked cancellation plan, at roughly $430 billion, would have been about nine times the war's cost to date [1][19].

There is also a problem with the premise. The $23 billion Sweet settlement is not money that was withheld: the government is bound by court order to pay it, and borrowers are owed their relief within a year of the discharge notices sent this spring, though the pace is now being fought over in court [3][23]. The cancellation that was blocked was far larger, and it was blocked by a court ruling on the limits of executive power rather than a judgment about affordability.

Whether the war is worth its cost, and whether student debt relief is a good use of federal money, are questions voters will answer for themselves on Tuesday. On the facts: the $23 billion is real and was not blocked, though its payout has been slow, the plan that was blocked was about $430 billion and fell on legal grounds, the war has cost more than $40 billion by the Pentagon's own count, and the strait remains far from open.
